turns.content: ok so when does a pattern of forgetting become a pattern of exclusion. like if someone always forgets your dietary needs and also forgets to put you in the group chat. at what point is it not just accidents anymore.

A pattern of forgetting becomes a pattern of exclusion when **the forgetting is predictable, repeatedly disadvantages you, and doesn’t change after it’s been clearly addressed**.

A single missed dietary need or group-chat invite can be an accident. But pay attention when:

- It keeps happening to **you**, while they reliably remember other people.
- The omissions consistently affect your ability to participate.
- You’ve explained the impact and made the solution easy, but nothing changes.
- They minimize it: “You’re overreacting,” “It’s not a big deal.”
- They apologize, yet make no practical adjustment.
- You’re expected to keep reminding, checking, and repairing everything yourself.
- You start feeling like your inclusion depends on being unusually vigilant.

Intent can remain unclear. Someone may be disorganized, overwhelmed, or genuinely forgetful—but **unintentional exclusion is still exclusion in effect**. The useful question isn’t only “Are they doing this deliberately?” It’s also: **“Once they know this hurts and excludes me, do they take reasonable steps to prevent it?”**

You could say:

> “I know each incident might seem accidental, but together they’re becoming a pattern. When my dietary needs are repeatedly forgotten and I’m left out of the group chat, I can’t fully participate. I need you to take concrete steps to include me—not just apologize afterward.”

Then ask for something observable: add you to the chat now, put your dietary needs in the shared notes, designate someone to check invitations. Their response—and especially what happens afterward—will tell you more than debating their intent.

You don’t need proof of malice before deciding that a relationship or group isn’t making enough room for you.
